analysis.one_liner: Writes a presidential order shielding energy producers from state climate laws into permanent federal law.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Judiciary Committee on July 23, 2025, the bill has sat there with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote, backed by 1 sponsor and 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill gives the force of federal law to Executive Order 14260, a 2025 presidential order aimed at state laws that burden oil, gas, and coal producers — including state climate liability laws that make energy companies pay for climate-related damages. Codifying it would keep those protections in place even if a future president tried to withdraw the order. The bill has only been referred to committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies. Executive Order 14260 directs the federal government to challenge state laws that penalize or target energy producers, and writing it into law would make that shield permanent: states could no longer use their own courts and laws to impose climate damages, cleanup costs, or penalties on the industry. Energy companies also gain because federal law is harder to undo than a presidential order, which the next administration could simply revoke.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes Executive Order 14260 — the 'Protecting American Energy from State Overreach' order — have the force and effect of law, rather than remaining an order that a future president could withdraw.

Executive Order 14260, which the bill incorporates, is aimed at state laws that 'burden' American energy production, including state climate-liability laws that require energy companies to pay for climate damages.

analysis.who_pays: State governments and their residents. If state climate-liability and cleanup laws are preempted, the costs that those laws would have shifted to energy companies — from climate damage compensation to environmental remediation — stay with state taxpayers instead. States also lose their own authority to set consumer and energy policies that conflict with federal policy.

drawbacks.text: Preempting state climate-liability laws means costs that states had tried to assign to energy producers — such as compensation for climate-related damage — would instead fall on state budgets and residents.
Codifying the order would permanently override the ability of individual states to set their own laws on energy, liability, and disclosure, concentrating that authority at the federal level.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a clear, permanent benefit to one industry — protection from state lawsuits and penalties — while shifting the corresponding costs onto state taxpayers and removing state authority to legislate on energy and liability. There is no offsetting mechanism in the bill for the public costs it creates.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and it has not been taken up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Troy Balderson introduced the bill on July 23, 2025, with Rep. Harriet Hageman as an original cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
As of the latest action record, no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained from the bill itself, since it has not advanced. If it never moves, state climate-liability authority remains intact and energy companies remain exposed to it.

for.name: Rep. Troy Balderson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify Executive Order 14260.

for.name: Rep. Harriet Hageman
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrats have signed on, and the bill has drawn no recorded opposition actions in either chamber.

industries.note: Codifying the order would permanently shield these companies from state climate-liability laws, penalties, and enforcement actions, meaning damages those laws would have made them pay stay with the public instead. Because federal law is harder to reverse than a presidential order, the shield outlasts the administration that issued it.

The measure overrides state laws and state court claims targeting energy producers, stripping states of authority they have used to impose climate damages and cleanup obligations. Residents bear the shifted costs.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, four cosponsors, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill follows the typical path of a codification measure without leadership backing: it is likely to remain in committee for the rest of the Congress unless its provisions are folded into a larger energy package.
